then.text: Come back on a calm day and I'll take you out to see the gannets dive. They go in like arrows. It's the best free show in Connacht.
The tide's on the turn and so's the weather. If you fancy a rematch, now's the time, before the gannets get cheeky.

else.text: Once a day, a chara. Even the tide takes a breather between turns. Tomorrow.
Another time, then. The offer stands.
Dia dhuit. You've walked a long way to my quay. Mind the nets. And the cat. The cat has right of way.
The tide's turning. It always is, in Galway. I've rowed a currach out past the Aran Islands in worse than you.
Tide creatures are patient and then they're not. Ready?
The Tide Stone. It comes in, it goes out, and in between it tells you who you are. That's what my grandmother said, and she rowed to Inis Mór in a gale.
Go n-éirí an bóthar leat. That's 'may the road rise with you'. It'll rise. Watch the bay at dusk. The light goes silver and the whole city stops to look.
Your phone buzzes. Professor Garside, who sounds as if she is standing in an airport.
{player}! The Tide Stone! Seven! I've lost count and then found it again, under a biscuit tin.
Kerrigan's booked Newgrange for the winter solstice. It's the big one. The passage fills with light for a few minutes, once a year, at dawn.
The bog road north is open now. Sligo, then the Boyne Valley, then the tomb. Or you could go the long way, back through Dublin. The road's reopened for that, too.
I'll meet you there. Yes, in person. I have a passport. It's been in a drawer since the eighties and it has a very surprised photograph.
Out in the town, the Wardens at the bog road finished their consultation and went to look at the boats.

then.text: There are four classes of hooker: the Bád Mór, the Leathbhád, the Gleoteog and the Púcán. Every August the hookers gather at Kinvara for Cruinniú na mBád, and the whole bay turns black and tan.

else.text: Race of the Waves? 1931, was it? My granda talked about it. A hooker will sail it, as a committee boat, if the Gaeltacht crews can be got to row. Try the Irish college at Gweedore.
I only take a lad's word on a boat after he has looked it over. Have a look at the old hooker on the water first, and read what is on her tiller.

arc_ie_steward.text: Rás na dTonnta, the Race of the Waves. A hooker is the committee boat now, and I am the committee. The committee is me.

then.text: For the crew that gathered us. Eat it before the gulls notice.
